Your updated, interview-ready reference — the notebook, cleaned up for 2026, now one page with a tab per topic and a flow diagram in each. Pick a topic above, search, and rehearse.

Updated Nov 2026OAuth 2.1 · NIST 800-63-4For: IAM interviews

The whole model — one request, three questions

Userwants to open an app or call an API
IdP vouchesSAML assertion or OIDC ID token — “this is Vinay, proofed at IAL2”
User provesPasskey / WebAuthn ceremony — private key signs a fresh challenge
Policy permitsOAuth scopes + claims + context decide what the token may do
App / APIvalidates, then serves — never trusts an unvalidated token
01 — Federation

Who vouches?

The IdP asserts identity. SAML for legacy enterprise XML assertions, OIDC for modern JSON / mobile. Trust = metadata, signing keys, issuer.

02 — Authentication

Who proves?

The user proves possession / knowledge / inherence. Today: passkeys / WebAuthn first, then OTP, push, magic link as fallbacks by assurance level.

03 — Authorization

Who permits?

OAuth 2.0 delegates access. Scopes + claims + policies decide what a token can do — authentication alone never grants access.

Your 30-second opener

“Authentication answers three questions: who vouches — federation with SAML or OIDC; who proves — increasingly a passkey, not a password; and who permits — OAuth scopes and policy. Get those three layers separate in your head, and every product — Okta, Entra, Ping — is just a different implementation of the same model.”

SAML 2.0

Enterprise federation workhorse — from the notebook, cleaned up

What it is

XML-based standard for transferring identity between two parties: the IdP performs authentication and passes the user’s identity and authorization level to the SP; the SP trusts the IdP and authorizes the user for the requested resource. SAML vs OIDC in the notebook’s own shorthand: old / XML / monolithic / heavy / web-based vs new / JSON / micro-services / light-weight / mobile & native.

Assertion statements — only two in practice: AuthnStatement (authentication) · AttributeStatement (attributes)Bindings: HTTP-POST · HTTP-RedirectExamples — SP: Salesforce, Jira, AWS · IdP: Okta, Entra

Benefits to quote: increased security (single point of authentication in the IdP), better UX (no separate credentials per app), standard-based interoperability.

Bindings — HTTP-Redirect vs HTTP-POST

Bindings are how the browser carries the SAML message between SP and IdP. Same message, different transport.

In short — SP-initiated login

SPStarts the login
AuthnRequest via HTTP-Redirect → IdPThe SP sends the AuthnRequest via HTTP-Redirect to the IdP
Response via HTTP-POST → SP ACSThe IdP sends the Response containing the assertion via HTTP-POST back to the SP’s ACS endpoint
SPValidates the assertion, creates the session

One-liner: Redirect is a small signed note in the URL; POST is the sealed envelope — which is why requests go by Redirect and responses come back by POST.

HTTP-RedirectHTTP-POST
How it travelsMessage rides in the URL query string (SAMLRequest=…)Browser loads an auto-submitting HTML form that POSTs to the other party
EncodingDEFLATE-compressed, then Base64, then URL-encodedBase64 only, no compression
SizeLimited by URL length — fine for small requestsNo real limit — handles large assertions with many attributes
SigningMessage itself isn’t XML-signed; signature is separate query params (SigAlg + Signature)The XML message / assertion is signed inside the document itself
Encryption & exposureCan’t encrypt — visible in browser history and server logsAssertion can be encrypted
Used forSmall requests: AuthnRequest and LogoutRequestThe Response / assertion, and IdP-initiated SSO

Which binding is used when

MessageBindingWhy / note
AuthnRequest — SP → IdPRedirectSmall, fits in a URL. POST exception: if signed / large and both sides’ metadata supports POST.
SAML Response — IdP → SP (ACS)POSTBig, signed, can be encrypted — can’t fit in a URL.
IdP-initiated SSO — no requestPOST onlyNo request at all — the IdP sends the Response straight to the ACS.
LogoutRequest — SP → IdPRedirectSmall, same as an AuthnRequest.
LogoutResponseEitherRedirect or POST — both are small enough; metadata decides.

What decides it in the end is metadata — the IdP’s SingleSignOnService endpoints and the SP’s AssertionConsumerService endpoints each declare which bindings they accept. You use a binding that appears in both. In a trace: SAMLRequest in a URL = the SP asking; a form POST with SAMLResponse = the IdP answering.

SP-initiated flow

User starts at the app

  1. 1User → SPLogs in / requests a resource at Salesforce
  2. 2SP → UserSAML Request generated, browser redirected to the IdP
  3. 3User → IdPSAML Request delivered; IdP authenticates the user (+ MFA)
  4. 4IdP → UserSigned SAML Assertion issued
  5. 5User → SPAssertion POSTed to the SP’s Assertion Consumer Service
  6. 6SPValidates signature, issuer, audience, expiry → session created

IdP-initiated flow

User starts at the IdP portal

  1. 1User → IdPLogs in at the IdP (e.g. Okta dashboard), clicks the app tile
  2. 2IdPBuilds an unsolicited SAML Assertion — no AuthnRequest preceded it
  3. 3IdP → User → SPAssertion POSTed straight to the SP’s ACS endpoint
  4. 4SPValidates and creates the session — must guard replay carefully, there is no request to correlate

Interview trap: IdP-initiated is convenient but weaker — no InResponseTo correlation, so lean harder on assertion ID one-time-use, short validity windows, and audience restriction.

Circle of trust — metadata exchange

Trust is established before any login happens

IdP metadataEntity ID · X.509 signing cert · SingleSignOnService endpoint · NameID format
Exchanged & imported both waysEach side loads the other’s metadata — that exchange is the trust
SP metadataEntity ID · SP cert · AssertionConsumerService endpoint (HTTP-POST) · NameID format

Optional fields that bite in production: WantAuthnRequestsSigned, SingleLogoutService, AuthnRequestsSigned, WantAssertionsSigned, ValidUntil. NameID “unspecified” = the IdP decides the format — pin it down explicitly in real integrations.

Watch list: assertion replay, clock skew, XML signature wrapping, unsolicited (IdP-init) responses. Interview line: “SAML and OIDC solve the same federation problem — SAML is XML, POST-bound, enterprise-proven; OIDC is JSON, REST-friendly, and wins on mobile / native.”

OIDC & OAuth 2.0 / 2.1

Identity layer vs delegation layer — never merge them

OpenID Connect — identity layer on OAuth 2.0

Use when: modern web, mobile, SPA, CIAM. Returns an ID token (JWT) for who the user is, plus an access token for APIs.

Discovery: /.well-known/openid-configurationJWKS for key rotationUserInfo endpoint

OIDC login flow (Authorization Code)

1 · /authorizeApp redirects user to IdP with scope=openid, state, nonce
2 · AuthenticateIdP logs the user in (+ passkey / MFA), gets consent
3 · CodeIdP redirects back with a short-lived, single-use code
4 · /tokenBack-channel exchange → ID token + access token (+ refresh)
5 · /userinfo + APIsValidate ID token first; access token calls APIs
GET /authorize?response_type=code
  &client_id=… &redirect_uri=… &scope=openid profile email
  &code_challenge=… &code_challenge_method=S256
  &nonce=… &state=…

POST /token  →  id_token + access_token + refresh_token
GET  /userinfo  (Bearer access_token)

Validate ID token: signature via JWKS, iss, aud, exp, nonce. Never trust claims before validation.

OAuth 2.0 → 2.1 — delegated authorization, not login

Use when: an app needs limited access to an API on someone’s behalf. OAuth alone does not tell you who logged in — that’s OIDC’s job.

✕ Implicit flow — removed in 2.1✕ ROPC / password grant — removed✓ Auth Code + PKCE for all clients✓ Exact redirect URI match

Which grant for which client

Auth Code + PKCEHumans in browsers, mobile, SPAs — the default
Client CredentialsMachine-to-machine, no user present
Device CodeTVs, CLIs, input-constrained devices
Refresh TokenLong sessions — only with rotation (see Tokens tab)

2.1 consolidates best practice — it’s not a new wire protocol.

SAML vs OIDC vs OAuth — the comparison table

SAMLOIDCOAuth 2.0
QuestionWho are you?Who are you?What may you do?
FormatXML assertionJWT ID tokenAccess token (JWT or opaque)
Best forEnterprise SaaS SSOWeb / mobile / CIAMAPI delegation
Watch outXML sig complexityNonce / state omissionUsing it as login alone

Auth Code + PKCE flow

The flow to be able to draw from memory

Full flow at a glance

  1. 1AppGenerates code_verifier (random, 43–128 chars), hashes it → code_challenge. Verifier stays on the device.
  2. 2App → IdPRedirect to /authorize with code_challenge + S256, state (CSRF), nonce (replay).
  3. 3IdPAuthenticates the user, gets consent, issues a short-lived single-use code.
  4. 4IdP → AppRedirect back: ?code=…&state=… — app verifies state matches exactly.
  5. 5App → IdPPOST /token with code + code_verifier (back channel). IdP re-hashes — must equal step 1’s challenge. This is the PKCE check.
  6. 6IdP → AppTokens issued. App validates the ID token, stores tokens securely, refresh rotates on use.

Step through it

Why PKCE? It binds the code to the device that started the flow — so an intercepted code is useless. Originally for public clients (mobile/SPA), now required for all clients in OAuth 2.1, including confidential ones as defence-in-depth.

JWT lab

Anatomy first, then decode & validate

Anatomy of a JWT

HeadereyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs…. Payload · claimseyJpc3MiOiJodHRwczov…. SignatureSflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4…

Header = algorithm + key ID (kid) → which JWKS key verifies it. Payload = claims: iss, sub, aud, exp, iat, nonce, scope. Signature = header + payload signed by the IdP’s private key. Base64URL-encoded, not encrypted — anyone can read the first two parts.

Header will appear here
Payload will appear here
  • ✓Verify signature against IdP JWKS — never alg: none, pin allowed algs
  • ✓Check iss exactly, aud contains your client_id, exp / nbf / iat within clock skew
  • ✓For OIDC: check nonce; for access tokens: check scope / scp and audience per-API
  • ✓A JWT is encoded, not encrypted — never put secrets or PII you wouldn’t print

Passkeys & WebAuthn

The 2026 centrepiece — both ceremonies, as sequence diagrams

Registration ceremony

navigator.credentials.create()

  1. 1User → Relying PartyOpens the site, clicks Register
  2. 2RP → BrowserServer generates a fresh challenge; page calls credentials.create() with it
  3. 3Browser → AuthenticatorChallenge + “create new credential” command passed to the authenticator
  4. 4AuthenticatorUser authorizes (biometric / PIN) → new key pair created, private key stays on device
  5. 5Authenticator → RPPublic key + credential ID + signed challenge (+ attestation, if requested)
  6. 6RPStores public key + credential ID against the account → Registered

Authentication ceremony

navigator.credentials.get()

  1. 1User → Relying PartyOpens the site, clicks Log in
  2. 2RP → BrowserNew single-use challenge; page calls credentials.get() with allowed credential IDs
  3. 3Browser → AuthenticatorChallenge + get-credentials command
  4. 4AuthenticatorUser authorizes → private key signs the challenge; sign-count increments
  5. 5Authenticator → RPSigned challenge returned
  6. 6RPVerifies signature with stored public key, checks challenge freshness + sign-count (clone detection) → Logged in

Synced passkeys

Private key syncs via iCloud Keychain / Google Password Manager. Best UX, cross-device recovery built in.

Consumer / CIAMAAL2 capable*

*Per NIST 800-63B / -63-4 guidance, depends on sync fabric controls. Enterprises that need strict device binding may not accept them for high assurance.

Device-bound passkeys

Key never leaves one authenticator — security key (YubiKey) or platform TPM. Strongest binding, harder recovery.

Workforce / high assuranceAttestation matters here

Use attestation to verify authenticator model in regulated / workforce enrolment — rarely in consumer, where it adds friction and privacy concerns. Platform authenticators are built in; roaming authenticators connect over USB / Bluetooth / NFC.

Interview trap: “Are passkeys biometrics?” No. Biometrics (Face ID / fingerprint) only unlock the private key locally — biometric data never leaves the device and is never sent to the server. WebAuthn is not a federation protocol: it’s how the authenticator proves you, and it pairs with any IdP as a factor or primary login.

Lifecycle, SCIM & linking

Getting the account there before login — and removing it on time

Joiner · Mover · Leaver — the lifecycle diagram

One identity, three events that drive everything

JoinerHR creates the record → account provisioned, birthright access granted, first login ready day one
MoverRole / dept changes → entitlements updated, old access removed — not just new access added
LeaverExit event → accounts disabled same day, sessions revoked, tokens killed, access certified closed

SCIM 2.0 provisioning flow

How accounts actually travel

  1. 1HR systemAuthoritative source fires a Joiner / Mover / Leaver event
  2. 2IdP / IGAEvaluates policy: which apps, which groups, which entitlements
  3. 3SCIM client → AppPOST /Users to create, PATCH /Users/{id} to update, DELETE / deactivate to deprovision — groups via /Groups
  4. 4AppAccount exists before first login; reconciliation catches drift and orphans

SCIM ≠ authentication. SCIM gets the account there before first login; SAML/OIDC proves it at login. Know: PATCH vs PUT, filtering, bulk operations, error handling / reconciliation.

JIT & account linking

JIT provisioning: create the local account on first federated login from assertion claims — no SCIM pre-provision needed.

Social + linking: match on verified email only, prompt to link, never auto-merge on unverified claims — that’s an account-takeover path.

Linking decision flow

  1. 1UserSigns in with a social / external IdP
  2. 2SPEmail claim verified? If not → no match, no merge
  3. 3SP → UserVerified email matches an existing account → prompt to link, re-authenticate
  4. 4SPIdentities linked; the IdP delegates proof, the SP still owns session and policy

Zero Trust & assurance

NIST 800-63 — and how a policy decision actually happens

Policy decision flow

Every request, evaluated fresh — never trust by network location

Signals inIdentity assurance · device posture · IP / geo velocity · behaviour · risk score
Policy engineCompares signals against the resource’s required assurance (IAL / AAL / FAL)
Decision outOne of four outcomes, below — enforced at the app / gateway, logged for audit
Allow
Step-up auth
Limit / read-only
Deny

Your bridge line: Okta network-zone policy — MFA outside the enterprise network — was an early, coarse version of this. Zero Trust is the same idea with far richer signals and per-request evaluation.

LevelMeansExample
IAL — Identity AssuranceHow strongly identity was proofed at enrolmentIAL2: document + biometric check
AAL — Authenticator AssuranceHow strongly login is authenticatedAAL2: two factors / passkey; AAL3: hardware-bound, verifier-impersonation resistant
FAL — Federation AssuranceHow strongly the assertion is protectedSigned + encrypted assertions, holder-of-key

Token security & DPoP

2026 additions — sender-constraining is the headline

DPoP — Demonstrating Proof of Possession (RFC 9449)

One line: a bearer token works for whoever holds it. A DPoP token only works for whoever holds the private key it was bound to.

DPoP flow — issuance, use, and the stolen-token test

  1. 1AppGenerates a key pair on the device — private key in secure enclave / WebCrypto, non-extractable, never leaves.
  2. 2App → Auth serverToken request carries a DPoP proof: a small JWT signed by the private key, public key in its header (jwk).
  3. 3Auth server → AppAccess token issued with the key’s thumbprint embedded: "cnf": { "jkt": "0ZcOCORZNYy-DWpqq30jZyJGHTN0d2HglBV3uiguA4I" }
  4. 4App → APIEach request sends Authorization: DPoP <token> plus a fresh proof binding method (htm), URL (htu), timestamp (iat), unique jti, and a hash of the token (ath).
  5. 5APIChecks: proof signature matches the token’s jkt + method/URL match + proof is fresh + jti unseen. Fail any one → reject.
  6. 6AttackerSteals the token from logs / a proxy and replays it from another machine → rejected. No private key, no proof. Stolen token, useless token.
GET /v1/accounts HTTP/1.1
Host: api.bank.com
Authorization: DPoP eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIs...   ← DPoP, not Bearer
DPoP: eyJ0eXAiOiJkcG9wK2p3dCIsImFsZyI6IkVTMjU2Ii...

DPoP proof payload:
{ "jti": "unique-id", "htm": "GET",
  "htu": "https://api.bank.com/v1/accounts",
  "iat": 1763840000, "ath": "hash-of-the-access-token" }

Because htm / htu / iat are inside the proof, you can’t replay the proof itself on a different endpoint or ten minutes later. Where it lands: open banking / FAPI 2.0, SPAs and mobile apps calling high-value APIs — payments, profile changes, anywhere a leaked token = account takeover.

DPoP vs mTLS — the trap question

DPoPmTLS-bound token
Proof isA signed JWT per request, at the app layerThe TLS client certificate, at transport layer
Through proxies / CDNsWorks — survives TLS terminationOften breaks — TLS gets terminated
Best forBrowser, mobile, public clientsServer-to-server, workloads

Both are sender-constraining — DPoP is just the one that survives the modern web stack.

Refresh token rotation

Rotation + reuse detection

  1. 1App → IdPPresents refresh token RT₁ → gets access token + new refresh token RT₂. RT₁ is retired.
  2. 2IdPIf RT₁ ever reappears → someone copied it → revoke the whole token family, force re-auth.

Short access-token lifetimes (5–15 min for sensitive APIs); refresh tokens only where a secure store exists.

PAR + RAR & revocation reality

PAR (Pushed Authorization Requests): auth parameters go back-channel, browser carries only a reference — nothing sensitive in the URL. RAR: rich, structured authorization details instead of flat scope strings.

Stateless JWTs can’t be instantly revoked — mitigate with short expiry, token introspection for high-risk calls, and event-driven signals (Continuous Access Evaluation / Shared Signals) to kill sessions mid-flight.

Non-human & AI-agent identity

What hiring managers probe now

Delegation flow — an agent acting for a user

Token exchange (RFC 8693) — delegation, not impersonation

  1. 1User → AgentUser authenticates and asks the agent to do a task. The agent never receives the user’s full session or a long-lived key.
  2. 2Agent → Auth serverToken exchange: presents the user’s token + its own identity, requests a down-scoped token for this task only.
  3. 3Auth server → AgentNew short-lived token carrying both identities: sub = the user, act = the agent acting. Audit can separate the two.
  4. 4Agent → API / toolCalls with the scoped token — least privilege per task, per tool call.
  5. 5PolicyAction crosses a risk threshold → step-up / human approval before it proceeds — same pattern as contextual access for humans.
  • No long-lived secrets: workload identity federation / SPIFFE SVIDs — short-lived, attested credentials instead of static API keys in code.
  • Every workload is an identity: agents, services, and jobs outnumber humans — inventory, ownership, and lifecycle apply to them too.
  • Least privilege per task: scoped, short-lived, down-scoped tokens per tool call — not the user’s session handed over wholesale.

SPIFFE & SPIRE

Workload identity — attested, short-lived, no static secrets

Standard vs implementation — never merge them

SPIFFE — Secure Production Identity Framework For Everyone — is the open standard / specification: it defines how a workload gets a cryptographic identity and how other workloads verify it. SPIRE — SPIFFE Runtime Environment — is the production implementation of that standard: the server and agents that actually attest workloads and issue their identities.

SPIFFE = the specSPIRE = the runtime that implements itCNCF graduated projectReplaces static API keys & long-lived certs

The split in one line

SPIFFE — definesSPIFFE ID format · SVID document types · Trust bundles · Workload API contract
SPIRE — deliversAttestation plugins · Registration & policy · SVID minting, rotation & federation in a real fleet
Workload — consumesFetches its SVID over the Workload API and uses it for mTLS / token exchange — no secret ever stored

How SPIRE issues an identity — attestation flow

A workload starts with nothing — and proves what it is

  1. 1Workload startsA service, container, or job starts on a node with no password, API key, or pre-provisioned cert — there is nothing to steal at rest.
  2. 2SPIRE Agent → ServerNode attestation: the Agent on that node proves the node itself — e.g. a cloud instance identity document (AWS / GCP / Azure), a Kubernetes service account, or a TPM — and receives its own node SVID.
  3. 3SPIRE AgentWorkload attestation: the Agent inspects the calling workload’s properties — PID, container image, Kubernetes pod / namespace / service account, Unix UID — and derives its selectors.
  4. 4Agent ↔ ServerSelectors are matched against registration entries on the Server (created by an admin or automation). A match authorises exactly one SPIFFE ID for that workload — no match, no identity.
  5. 5SPIRE Server → AgentServer signs and issues an SVID — the workload’s identity document — with a short TTL, typically minutes to hours.
  6. 6Agent → WorkloadSVID delivered over the Workload API on a local Unix domain socket. The Agent rotates it automatically before expiry and pushes the new one — the workload never handles renewal logic.
  7. ↺Workload → WorkloadEach side presents its SVID and validates the peer against the trust bundle → mutual TLS with cryptographic workload identity on both ends.

Architecture at a glance

SPIRE ServerControl plane · holds the CA, registration entries & trust bundle · signs SVIDs · one per trust domain (HA pair in production)
SPIRE AgentOne per node / host · attests node + workloads · caches & rotates SVIDs · exposes the Workload API socket
WorkloadYour service · fetches SVID via Workload API · uses it for mTLS or exchanges it for a cloud / OAuth token

SPIFFE ID & the SVID

Every workload gets a URI identity inside a trust domain:

spiffe://example.org/payments/charge-service
└─ trust domain ─┘ └──── workload path ────┘

The ID lives in the SVID — in an X.509 certificate it is the URI SAN, in a JWT it is the sub claim. The trust domain is the security boundary: workloads only trust SVIDs signed by their own domain’s bundle, unless domains are explicitly federated.

  • Registration entry = the policy record: SPIFFE ID + the selectors a workload must match + TTL.
  • Selectors = attested facts, not claims the workload makes about itself: k8s:ns:payments, k8s:sa:charge, docker:image-id:…
  • Short TTL by design — compromise window is the SVID’s remaining life, not the life of a leaked static key.

X.509-SVID vs JWT-SVID

X.509-SVIDJWT-SVID
FormCertificate + private keySigned JWT token
Used formTLS between workloads — the defaultCalling APIs / crossing layers where TLS client certs don’t fit
AudienceAny peer in the trust domainBound to a specific aud — request one per audience
Watch outKey stays in memory / socket, never on disk by defaultIt is a bearer token — theft risk until expiry, so keep TTL very short

Rule of thumb to quote: X.509-SVID for workload-to-workload mTLS, JWT-SVID when a workload must authenticate to something that only speaks tokens.

Federation — crossing trust domains

Two domains, mutual trust by bundle exchange

Domain Aspiffe://corp.example — its bundle = its CA roots
Bundle exchangeEach domain publishes / fetches the other’s trust bundle — that exchange is the federation, like SAML metadata
Domain Bspiffe://partner.example — workloads there can now validate A’s SVIDs, and vice versa
  • Where it lands: Kubernetes multi-cluster services, cloud workloads (exchange an SVID for an AWS / GCP / Azure token via workload identity federation), service meshes, CI/CD jobs, and AI agents / NHI — any non-human actor that today would hold a static secret.
  • vs OAuth client credentials: client credentials still start from a stored secret. SPIFFE bootstraps from attestation — identity is proven from the environment, never from a secret the workload was given.
  • vs plain mTLS: mTLS is the transport; SPIFFE decides who gets the cert, what identity is inside it, and how it rotates — the identity layer underneath the TLS.

“SPIFFE answers for workloads what OIDC answers for people — a standard, verifiable identity. SPIRE is how you run it: attest the node, attest the workload, mint a short-lived SVID, rotate it forever — and delete the static secret entirely.”

Okta

Vendor tab — Workforce Identity & Okta CIAM

Sign-on flow through the Okta Identity Engine (OIE)

One request through the OIE pipeline

  1. 1User → AppOpens an app → redirected to Okta (OIDC /authorize or SAML AuthnRequest)
  2. 2OktaGlobal session policy evaluates: network zone, device, risk signals (ThreatInsight, behaviour)
  3. 3OktaAuthentication policy for that app decides which authenticators are required — password, Okta Verify, passkey / WebAuthn
  4. 4OktaClaims assembled: profile attributes + group memberships mapped into the assertion / tokens
  5. 5Okta → AppID token + access token from the authorization server (or SAML assertion) → app session
  6. ↺In parallelProvisioning arm: HR source → Okta profile → SCIM / lifecycle states push accounts to downstream apps (Joiner / Mover / Leaver)

OIE is the default engineClassic is retired — don’t quote itTerraform provider = config as codeOkta Workflows = no-code automationIdentity Governance: certifications & entitlements

  • Policies are the product: global session → app authentication → MFA enrolment. If you can explain policy evaluation order, you can explain Okta.
  • Network zones are your Zero Trust bridge story: MFA outside the enterprise zone was contextual access before it had the name.
  • Config as code: apps, policies, and groups managed in Terraform with GitOps review — the pattern you ran at Salesforce / Trailblazer scale.
  • Retired — never present as current: OPP agent, SCIM 1.1, Classic engine and its sid cookie model.

“Okta is a policy engine with an identity store attached — the pipeline is policy → authenticators → claims → tokens, and everything else is configuration.”

SailPoint

Vendor tab — Identity Governance & Administration (IGA)

Governance flow — source to certification to provisioning

How an identity gets governed end to end

  1. 1Authoritative sourceHR system (e.g. Workday) feeds identities — the single source of truth for who exists
  2. 2AggregationConnectors pull accounts & entitlements from every target app and correlate them to identities
  3. 3Identity cubeOne governed view per person: accounts, entitlements, roles, risk — the thing every decision reads from
  4. 4GovernanceAccess requests, role mining, SoD policy checks, and certification campaigns run against the cube
  5. 5ProvisioningApproved changes pushed back out through connectors — Joiner / Mover / Leaver executed, with an audit trail

IdentityIQ — on-prem, deep customisationIdentity Security Cloud (ex-IdentityNow) — SaaSCertifications / access reviewsSoD policiesAI-assisted role mining & recommendations

  • The distinction that matters: Okta/Entra authenticate and provision; SailPoint governs — who should have access, who approved it, who reviewed it.
  • Certification campaigns are the audit answer: managers attest access is still needed, revocations feed straight back into provisioning.
  • SoD (separation of duties): toxic combinations — e.g. create vendor + pay vendor — blocked at request time, not found at audit time.
  • Your delivery story: 25+ IGA programs at Focal Point with IdentityIQ / IdentityNow and CyberArk integration — governance wired to privileged access, not a standalone review tool.

“SailPoint answers the auditor’s question — not ‘can they log in?’ but ‘should they have it, who said so, and when was it last reviewed?’”

Microsoft Entra ID

Vendor tab — formerly Azure AD

Sign-in flow with Conditional Access evaluation

Signals in, grant controls out

  1. 1User → Entra IDSign-in request (OIDC / SAML) from an enterprise app or app registration
  2. 2Entra IDPrimary authentication — increasingly passwordless: passkey / FIDO2, Windows Hello, Authenticator
  3. 3Conditional AccessPolicies evaluate signals: user & sign-in risk (Identity Protection), device compliance (Intune), location, client app
  4. 4Grant controlsRequire MFA / compliant device / approved client — or block. Session controls can limit what the session may do
  5. 5Entra ID → AppToken issued with claims (groups, roles, amr, device state) → app authorizes
  6. ↺Admin armPIM: admins hold no standing privilege — eligible roles are activated just-in-time, time-boxed, with approval and audit

Conditional Access = the policy enginePIM — just-in-time elevationEntra ID Governance: entitlement management + access reviewsExternal ID — B2B / CIAMPasskeys & CBA supported as authenticators

  • Conditional Access is Entra’s centrepiece — the Zero Trust policy decision from the Zero Trust tab, productised: signals → policy → grant controls.
  • App model: app registrations (the app’s identity) vs enterprise apps / service principals (its instance in your tenant) — know the difference cold.
  • Governance parity: entitlement management access packages + scheduled access reviews are Entra’s answer to SailPoint-style certification, inside the Microsoft stack.
  • Federation both ways: Entra can be IdP (SAML/OIDC to apps) or sit behind / federate with Okta — per-app MFA scoping follows the session owner, a point you know from the Citrix Workspace work.

“Entra ID’s story is Conditional Access: every sign-in is a policy decision made from risk, device, and location signals — not a password check.”

CyberArk

Vendor tab — Privileged Access Management (PAM)

Privileged session flow — vault, isolate, rotate

The admin never sees the password

  1. 1Admin → PVWARequests a privileged session and gives a reason; policy checks entitlement, time window, approval / dual control
  2. 2VaultReleases the credential to the session broker only — the password is never displayed or copied to the admin’s machine
  3. 3PSMPrivileged Session Manager opens an isolated session to the target and injects the credential — fully recorded, keystrokes logged
  4. 4TargetAdmin works inside the isolated session; file transfer and commands can be restricted by policy
  5. 5CPMSession ends → Central Policy Manager rotates the password automatically. The credential the session used no longer exists

Vault — credential storeCPM — rotation enginePSM / PSMP — session isolation & recordingEPM — endpoint least privilegeSecrets Manager / Conjur — workload & NHI secrets

  • Core principle: eliminate standing, known credentials. Vault them, broker their use, rotate after every use.
  • EPM extends the same idea to endpoints: remove local admin rights, elevate per-application just-in-time — the endpoint-privilege pattern behind the Workday role you prepped for.
  • NHI angle: Secrets Manager / Conjur gives applications and pipelines short-lived, policy-controlled secrets instead of embedded API keys — ties straight into the Agents & NHI tab.
  • Integration story: CyberArk behind the IdP (SAML/OIDC + MFA into PVWA) and governed by IGA — your Focal Point pattern: SailPoint governs who may request, CyberArk enforces how the credential is used.

“CyberArk assumes the credential is the target — so the human never holds it, the session is recorded, and the password dies when the session does.”

PKI & Certificates

The passport office — the trust underneath every signature on this page

What it is

A certificate binds a public key to an identity, signed by a Certificate Authority (CA) you trust. Everything else in modern identity signs with keys those certificates vouch for — TLS server certs, SAML / OIDC signing keys, code signing, workload certs. PKI is the layer that makes “verify the signature” mean something: the signature is only as good as your trust in the key, and the certificate is that trust, written down.

The trust chain — leaf, intermediate, root

Leaf certificateThe end entity: a server, a user, a workload. Holds the public key + identity (subject / SANs). Short-lived by design.
Intermediate CASigns leaf certs day to day. Kept online but scoped — if it is compromised, revoke it and the damage stops there.
Root CASelf-signed anchor in the trust store. Kept offline, used rarely, guarded hardest — its compromise breaks everything under it.

A verifier walks the chain leaf → intermediate → root and checks each signature, expiry, and key usage. mTLS is this in both directions: server and client present certs, both chains verified.

X.509 — the certificate formatSANs carry the names (DNS / URI / SPIFFE ID)Key usage / EKU — what the key may doPrivate keys live in HSMs / key stores — never in repos

Certificate lifecycle — where PKI actually fails

From request to retirement

  1. 1RequesterGenerates a key pair and a CSR (certificate signing request) — the private key never leaves the requester
  2. 2CA / RAValidates the identity claim — domain control (DV), organisation (OV), extended (EV) — then the CA signs and issues
  3. 3DeployCert installed where it's used: load balancer, server, device, workload. Inventory it — you cannot renew what you forgot exists
  4. 4RenewBefore expiry, not after: automate issuance and rotation (ACME — the Let's Encrypt protocol) so lifetimes can shrink safely
  5. ✕Revoke / expireCompromise or decommission → revoke; verifiers learn via CRL (signed list) or OCSP (live status check). Short lifetimes make revocation matter less — expiry does the work
  • The operational killer is expiry, not cryptography. Most certificate outages are a forgotten cert on a forgotten system. Automation + inventory + alerts beat any cipher debate.
  • Tie-in — signing keys everywhere: the SAML assertion signature and the JWT kid / JWKS model are PKI ideas — a key, vouched for, rotated on a schedule. A rotated IdP signing cert that the SP hasn't picked up is the classic federation outage.
  • Tie-in — certificate-based auth (CBA): Entra ID and others accept a client certificate as an authentication factor — the device or smartcard proves possession of the private key, phishing-resistant by the same origin / key logic as passkeys.
  • Tie-in — workloads: a SPIFFE X.509-SVID is a certificate — SPIFFE ID in the URI SAN, minted by the SPIRE server acting as CA, rotated in hours. PKI with the lifecycle automated all the way down.

“PKI creates trust: a certificate binds a public key to an identity — and the discipline is the lifecycle, because expiry, not attackers, is what usually breaks it.”

Authorization Models

RBAC, ABAC, PBAC — layered, never either/or

The layered stack — how production authorization is actually built

Each layer answers a different question

1 · RBAC baseline“What's your job?” Roles bundle the access a job needs — coarse, stable, auditable. Birthright access lands here.
2 · ABAC gate“What's true right now?” Attributes — user, resource, context — gate the sensitive stuff: this data, this device, this risk level.
3 · PBAC policy“What does policy say?” Rules written once as code, evaluated by a policy engine, versioned and tested like software.
4 · JIT elevation“For how long?” Privilege above the baseline is granted just-in-time, time-boxed, approved — never standing.

And across all four: deny wins, and simulate the policy before you ship it — an authorization change is a production change.

ModelDecision readsStrengthFailure mode
RBAC — role-basedThe roles assigned to the identitySimple to explain, review, and certify; maps to job functionsRole explosion — a new role per exception until nobody can review them
ABAC — attribute-basedAttributes of user, resource, action, and environment at request timeFine-grained and contextual — “managers may read reports from their own cost centre, on a compliant device”Attribute quality — garbage attributes, garbage decisions; hard to answer “who can do X?”
PBAC — policy-basedCentral policy rules (OPA / Rego, Cedar, vendor engines) over roles + attributes + contextOne decision point, policy as code: testable, versioned, consistent across appsThe engine becomes critical infrastructure — latency, availability, and policy bugs ship everywhere at once

Key points

  • “RBAC or ABAC?” is the trap question. The senior answer is layered: RBAC for the baseline everyone can reason about, ABAC where data sensitivity or context demands it, PBAC when multiple apps must share one decision logic.
  • SoD lives in this layer. Separation of duties is a policy constraint across entitlements — “no identity may hold both create-vendor and pay-vendor” — enforced preventively at grant time where the model allows it, detected in certification where it doesn't (see Lifecycle & SCIM and the SailPoint tab).
  • Authorization ≠ authentication, and ≠ the token. A valid token proves who presented it; the model decides what they may do to this resource, now. Scopes are a coarse first filter, not the decision.
  • Cloud is this, productised: AWS IAM is PBAC with an RBAC accent — policies as JSON, ABAC via tags, deny-wins evaluation (see the AWS IAM tab). Entra Conditional Access is the same thinking on the authentication side.
  • Reviewability is a design requirement. If you cannot list who can reach a sensitive resource and why, the model has failed — whatever it allows at runtime.

“RBAC answers ‘what's your job?’, ABAC answers ‘what's true right now?’, PBAC answers ‘what does the policy say?’ — production systems layer all three, then make privilege above the baseline just-in-time.”

Ping Identity

Vendor tab — the federation hub & token mediator

Federation flow — one hub, every protocol

A request through PingAccess + PingFederate

  1. 1User → AppRequests a protected web app or API
  2. 2PingAccessThe gateway / policy enforcement point checks the session and access policy — no valid session, the user is sent to authenticate
  3. 3PingFederateThe federation server runs its authentication policy: adapters chain primary auth, MFA (PingID or an external factor), and risk checks, and fill an authentication policy contract
  4. 4PingFederate — token mediationThe STS translates between worlds: a SAML assertion arrives from a partner IdP and an OAuth access token / OIDC ID token goes out to the app — or the reverse. Each side keeps speaking its own protocol
  5. 5App / APIReceives exactly the token format it understands, with attributes mapped from the contract — no app-side federation plumbing

PingFederate — self-hosted federation serverPingOne — the cloud IDaaS platformPingAccess — web & API access gatewayPingID — MFAPingDirectory — identity storeDaVinci — no-code orchestration (PingOne)

  • Ping's home turf is complex, hybrid federation: many partner IdPs, mixed SAML / OIDC / WS-Federation estates, and apps that each speak a different dialect. PingFederate sits in the middle and normalises all of it.
  • Token mediation is the headline feature: the Security Token Service issues, validates, and converts tokens across protocols and formats — the bridge that lets a legacy SAML estate serve modern OAuth / OIDC apps without rewriting either side.
  • Adapters are the extension model: authentication sources, MFA providers, and attribute stores plug in as adapters and are chained by policy — the same “policy decides” shape as Okta's OIE and Entra's Conditional Access, assembled differently.
  • PingFederate vs PingOne: Federate is the customer-run server (control, data residency, deep customisation); PingOne is the vendor-run cloud platform, with DaVinci for orchestrating journeys. Large enterprises often run both during a long hybrid transition.

“Ping is the federation plumber: PingFederate speaks every protocol dialect and mediates tokens between worlds that don't share one — legacy SAML in, OAuth out.”

AWS IAM

Vendor tab — cloud authorization, evaluated on every call

The gauntlet — how every AWS request is decided

Deny wins, ceilings limit, something must grant

  1. 1Explicit deny?Any applicable policy with an explicit Deny ends it here. Deny always wins, no exceptions
  2. 2SCP ceilingService Control Policies from AWS Organizations set the maximum permissions for the account — they limit, they never grant, and they bind every principal in the account
  3. 3Permission boundaryIf the principal has a permissions boundary, it caps what their identity policies can grant — the delegation guardrail that lets you hand out admin-of-a-sandbox safely
  4. 4A grantAn identity-based policy (on the user / role) or a resource-based policy (on the bucket, key, queue) must Allow the action — cross-account, both sides must allow
  5. ✓DecisionAllow only when no deny fires, every ceiling passes, and a grant exists. Otherwise it's an implicit deny — the default state of everything

Users / groups — legacy human patternRoles — temporary credentials, the defaultPolicies — JSON allow/deny documentsABAC — authorise by tagsIAM Access Analyzer — find the holes

  • Principals: IAM users (long-lived identities, often with access keys — the pattern to retire), groups (policy attachment buckets for users), and roles — assumable identities with short-lived credentials, used by workloads, cross-account access, and federated humans alike.
  • Workforce federation: humans don't get IAM users in a mature org. IAM Identity Center federates to Okta or Entra ID (SAML in, SCIM syncs users + groups), and a group + permission set + account assignment stamps a role into each account — disabling the person in Okta ends new access at the source.
  • ABAC in AWS: policies keyed on tags — principal tag must equal resource tag (project=blue opens project=blue) — so one policy scales as teams and resources grow, instead of one policy per project. Session tags can ride in from the IdP's attributes.
  • IAM Access Analyzer is the audit arm: it reasons over policies to flag resources shared outside the account / organisation, generates policies from actual CloudTrail usage (least privilege from evidence), and analyses unused access so standing permission can be cut.
  • The traps: saying SCPs grant access (they only cap); forgetting cross-account needs both sides to allow; IAM users + long-term keys as the human pattern; and locking tag editing down — if users can retag, ABAC becomes self-service privilege escalation.

“Deny wins, ceilings limit, something must grant — and the org's rules sit above every account.”
